evidence.title: Breed registry
evidence.text: A breed registry, also known as a herdbook, studbook or register, in animal husbandry and the hobby of animal fancy, is an official list of animals within a specific breed whose parents are known.

evidence.title: Breed registry
evidence.text: Animals are usually registered by their breeders when they are still young.

evidence.title: Breed registry
evidence.text: The terms "studbook" and "register" are also used to refer to lists of male animals "standing at stud", that is, those animals actively breeding, as opposed to every known specimen of that breed.

evidence.title: Breed registry
evidence.text: Such registries usually issue certificates for each recorded animal, called a pedigree, pedigreed animal documentation, or most commonly, an animal's "papers".

evidence.title: Breed registry
evidence.text: Registration papers may consist of a simple certificate or a listing of ancestors in the animal's background, sometimes with a chart showing the lineage.

evidence.title: Lonk
evidence.text: The Lonk is a domestic sheep of a specific breed, found in the hills of the central and south Pennines, in the north of England.

evidence.title: Lonk
evidence.text: The name "Lonk" derives from the Lancashire word "lanky", meaning long and thin, usually in a person.

evidence.title: Lonk
evidence.text: Their range extends into only three counties; Lancashire, Yorkshire and Derbyshire.

evidence.title: Lonk
evidence.text: Also known as the Improved Haslingden, the Lonk is of the Blackfaced Mountain type, and is similar to the Derbyshire Gritstone, apart from the absence of horns in that breed.

evidence.title: Oscar (bionic cat)
evidence.text: Oscar is an all black cat owned by Kate Allan and Mike Nolan who lives on the Channel Island of Jersey.

evidence.title: Oscar (bionic cat)
evidence.text: In 2009 Oscar had both hind paws severed by a combine harvester.

evidence.title: Oscar (bionic cat)
evidence.text: Since then he has undergone a pioneering operation to add prosthetic feet.

evidence.title: Oscar (bionic cat)
evidence.text: The treatment has since been considered for use with humans.

evidence.title: Oscar (bionic cat)
evidence.text: A book about Oscar's story, "Oscar the Bionic Cat" was published in 2013.

evidence.title: Nilgiri langur
evidence.text: The Nilgiri langur ("Trachypithecus johnii") is a lutung (a type of Old World monkey) found in the Nilgiri Hills of the Western Ghats in South India.

evidence.title: Nilgiri langur
evidence.text: Its range also includes Kodagu in Karnataka, Kodayar Hills in Tamil Nadu, and many other hilly areas in Kerala and Tamil Nadu.

evidence.title: Nilgiri langur
evidence.text: This primate has glossy black fur on its body and golden brown fur on its head.

evidence.title: Nilgiri langur
evidence.text: It is similar in size and long-tailed like the gray langurs. Females have a white patch of fur on the inner thigh.

evidence.title: Nilgiri langur
evidence.text: It typically lives in troops of nine to ten monkeys.

evidence.title: Nilgiri langur
evidence.text: Its diet consists of fruits, shoots and leaves.

evidence.title: Nilgiri langur
evidence.text: The species is classified as vulnerable due to habitat destruction and poaching for its fur and flesh, the latter believed to have aphrodisiac properties.

evidence.title: Breed club
evidence.text: Breed clubs are associations or clubs with activities centered on a single, specific breed of a particular species of domesticated animal.

evidence.title: Breed club
evidence.text: The purpose of the association will vary with the species of animal and the goals and needs of the members of the association.

evidence.title: Breed club
evidence.text: Breed associations or clubs may vary in their goals, activities and nomenclature from country to country, even for the same breed.

evidence.title: Breed club
evidence.text: Most domesticated animals, whether they are agricultural animals such as cattle, llamas, poultry, sheep and pigs, or companion animals such as pigeons, horses, cats and dogs, have breed clubs associated with the breed.

evidence.title: Puppy nutrition
evidence.text: The developmental life stage of dogs requires a specific intake of nutrients to ensure proper growth and development and to meet energy requirements.

evidence.title: Puppy nutrition
evidence.text: Despite the fact that puppies have different nutritional requirements compared to their adult counterparts, of the 652 breeders surveyed in the United States and Canada in 2012, 8.7% report feeding puppies commercial diets not intended for the developmental life stage of canines.

evidence.title: Puppy nutrition
evidence.text: Large and small dog breeds have even more specific nutrient requirements during growth, such as adjusted calcium to phosphorus ratio, and as such should receive a breed specific growth formula.

evidence.title: Puppy nutrition
evidence.text: Feeding diets formulated by a nutritionist for specific breed and life stage differences in nutrient requirements ensures a growing puppy will receive the proper nutrition associated with appropriate skeletal, neurological and immune development.

evidence.title: Puppy nutrition
evidence.text: This includes nutrients such as protein, fibre, essential fatty acids, calcium and vitamin E.

evidence.title: Puppy nutrition
evidence.text: It is therefore important to feed puppies a diet that meets the minimum and/or maximum requirements established by the National Research Council.

evidence.title: Carriage dog
evidence.text: A carriage dog or coach dog refers to a type of dog rather than a specific breed.

evidence.title: Carriage dog
evidence.text: Dogs of this type were usually bred and trained to trot alongside carriages to protect the occupants from banditry or other interference.

evidence.title: Carriage dog
evidence.text: They were usually owned and used by the wealthy or traders and merchants.

evidence.title: Carriage dog
evidence.text: The dogs were trained to attack the horses used by highwaymen, giving the owners' human security time to respond to the actual robbers.

evidence.title: Black cat
evidence.text: A black cat is a domestic cat with black fur that may be a mixed or specific breed.

evidence.title: Black cat
evidence.text: The Cat Fanciers' Association (CFA) recognizes 22 cat breeds that can come with solid black coats.

evidence.title: Black cat
evidence.text: The Bombay breed is exclusively black.

evidence.title: Black cat
evidence.text: All-black fur pigmentation is slightly more prevalent in male cats than female cats.

evidence.title: Black cat
evidence.text: Their high melanin pigment content causes most black cats to have yellow (golden) eyes (irises).

evidence.title: Karakul (hat)
evidence.text: A karakul (or qaraqul) hat (Pashto/Persian: قراقلی) is a hat made from the fur of the Qaraqul breed of sheep, often from the fur of aborted lamb foetuses.

evidence.title: Karakul (hat)
evidence.text: The triangular hat is part of the costume of the native people of Kabul which has been worn by many generations of men in Afghanistan.

evidence.title: Karakul (hat)
evidence.text: The fur from which it is made is referred to as "Astrakhan", "broadtail", "qaraqulcha", or "Persian lamb".

evidence.title: Karakul (hat)
evidence.text: Qaraqul means black fur in Turkic, similar types of hats are common among Turkic peoples.

evidence.title: Karakul (hat)
evidence.text: The hat is peaked, and folds flat when taken off of the wearer's head.

evidence.title: Kolpik
evidence.text: A kolpik is a type of traditional headgear worn in families of some Chassidic "rebbes" (Hasidic rabbis), by unmarried children on Shabbat, and by some "rebbes" on some special occasions other than Shabbat or major holidays.

evidence.title: Kolpik
evidence.text: The kolpik is made from brown fur, as opposed to a "spodik", worn by Polish chassidic dynasties, which is fashioned out of black fur.
